pos: adj. and n. (superlative of good; the choicest part; rendering Hebrew meytab and cheleb, Greek protos and kreitton)
etymology: Old English betst, the superlative that good borrowed from another root. In the Law the best of a thing is its fat, and the fat is the LORD's.
biblical_def: The best is the choicest part, and Scripture watches where it goes. The father says of the prodigal, “Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him” (Luk 15:22). Pharaoh gives Joseph's family “the best of the land” (Gen 47:6). The Levites are to heave to the LORD “the best thereof, even the hallowed part” (Num 18:29). Saul's army “spared the best of the sheep” God had devoted to destruction (1Sa 15:15). Paul says, “covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way” (1Co 12:31). Micah's verdict on a corrupt generation: “The best of them is as a brier” (Mic 7:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines best as most good; having good qualities in the highest degree; and, as a noun, the utmost, the highest endeavour.
webster_full: BEST, a. superlative. Most good; having good qualities in the highest degree; applicable to any person or thing.
2. Most advanced; most accurate; as the best scholar.
BEST, n. The utmost; the highest endeavor; as, to do one's best.
scriptures: But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet:
But covet earnestly the best gifts: and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way.
Out of all your gifts ye shall offer every heave offering of the LORD, of all the best thereof, even the hallowed part thereof out of it.
And Saul said, They have brought them from the Amalekites: for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the LORD thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed.
Mic 7:4
The best of them is as a brier: the most upright is sharper than a thorn hedge: the day of thy watchmen and thy visitation cometh; now shall be their perplexity.
corruption_summary: The best robe is preached as the father's soft-heartedness, and the best of the sheep as Saul's generosity.
corruption_paragraphs: The best robe in Luke 15 is not a gift a sentimental father could not help giving; it is a verdict. The son had rehearsed a speech ending in “make me as one of thy hired servants,” and the father did not let him finish it. The robe, the ring, and the shoes are the marks of a son, and the best robe — the first robe, the chief one in the house — is put on a man who smells of the swine. That is justification: not a cleaned-up sinner rewarded with a robe, but a filthy one clothed before he has washed. The elder brother's complaint in the field is the complaint of every religion of merit against grace.

Saul spared the best of the sheep and called it worship. “The people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the LORD thy God” — and Samuel's answer has outlived the kingdom: “to obey is better than sacrifice.” The best of what God has forbidden is not an offering; it is the disobedience, dressed. Numbers 18 is the honest version of the same word: the best is heaved to the LORD first, because it is His, and the man who keeps the best and gives the rest has read the verse backward.
roots_summary: Hebrew meytab (H4315), the best part; cheleb (H2459), fat, the choicest; tob (H2896), good; Greek protos (G4413), first, chief; kreitton (G2909), better, best.
roots_lines: Hebrew meytab (H4315) — the best, choicest; Genesis 47:6, 47:11, Exodus 22:5, 1 Samuel 15:9, 15:15.
Hebrew cheleb (H2459) — fat, and so the best; Numbers 18:12, 18:29–32.
Greek protos (G4413) — first, chief; Luke 15:22, the best robe; kreitton (G2909), better; 1 Corinthians 12:31.
usage: “Bring forth the best robe” — a son clothed before he has washed.
“Spared the best of the sheep” — disobedience dressed as an offering.
“Covet earnestly the best gifts” — and then the more excellent way.

pos: adj. (evil, worthless, rotten; rendering Hebrew ra, Greek sapros, poneros, and kakos)
etymology: Middle English badde, of uncertain descent. The Authorized Version uses the word sparingly and almost always in a pair: good or bad.
biblical_def: In Scripture bad nearly always stands beside good and marks a judgment between them. Laban and Bethuel “cannot speak unto thee bad or good” (Gen 24:50); Solomon asks for an understanding heart “that I may discern between good and bad” (1Ki 3:9); Jeremiah's figs are “very good” and “very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad” (Jer 24:2). The net gathers of every kind, and the fishermen “gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away” (Mat 13:48); the wedding is furnished with guests “both bad and good” (Mat 22:10). And at the judgment seat every one receives “the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad” (2Co 5:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bad as ill; not good; evil; vicious; wicked; unwholesome; unfortunate; a word of general application.
webster_full: BAD, a. Ill; not good; evil; vicious; wicked; the opposite of good.
2. Unwholesome; as bad air.
3. Unfortunate; unprosperous; as a bad state of affairs.
4. Imperfect; not sound; as a bad debt.
scriptures: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.
Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people?
So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.
Jer 24:2
One basket had very good figs, even like the figs that are first ripe: and the other basket had very naughty figs, which could not be eaten, they were so bad.
corruption_summary: Good and bad is treated as a spectrum with everyone somewhere in the middle, and the net in Matthew 13 has only two piles.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern morality prefers a gradient: nobody is bad, some are less good, and everyone is somewhere on the line. The parable of the net ends with two piles on the shore and nothing between them. “So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just.” The wedding hall in Matthew 22 was filled with bad and good together, and the king still walked the room and found the man without a garment. The gathering is indiscriminate; the sorting is not.

Second Corinthians 5:10 is addressed to Christians. Paul says “we must all appear,” and the reckoning is of things done in the body, good or bad. The doctrine of a judgment of works for the justified is not a threat to their justification — the same letter says they are new creatures and reconciled — but it is the reason Paul gives, in the very next verse, for persuading men: “Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord.” A gospel that has removed every consequence from the believer's conduct has removed the sentence Paul used to keep himself sober.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, bad, of poor quality; Greek sapros (G4550), rotten, worthless; poneros (G4190), evil; kakos (G2556), bad.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, bad, worthless; Genesis 24:50, 31:24, 1 Kings 3:9, Jeremiah 24:2, Leviticus 27:10.
Greek sapros (G4550) — rotten, unfit; Matthew 13:48, the bad fish; Matthew 7:17, the corrupt tree.
Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, wicked; Matthew 22:10; and kakos (G2556), 2 Corinthians 5:10.
usage: “Cast the bad away” — two piles on the shore.
“Whether it be good or bad” — the reckoning Paul kept before himself.
“Discern between good and bad” — what Solomon asked for instead of riches.

pos: adj. and adv. (smaller, fewer, inferior; rendering Hebrew me'at and ephes, Greek elachistoteros, elatton, and mikroteros)
etymology: Old English læssa, a comparative with no positive form of its own. Paul made a superlative of it — less than the least.
biblical_def: Paul coined a word for himself: “Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given” (Eph 3:8). Melchizedek is greater than Abraham because “without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better” (Heb 7:7). The nations before God “are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity” (Isa 40:17). The mustard seed “is less than all the seeds that be in the earth” (Mar 4:31). Ezra confesses that God “hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve” (Ezr 9:13), and Zophar tells Job that “God exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth” (Job 11:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines less as smaller, not so large or great; and, as an adverb, in a smaller or lower degree.
webster_full: LESS, a. Smaller; not so large or great; as a less quantity or number.
LESS, adv. Not so much; in a smaller or lower degree; as less bright or loud.
scriptures: Eph 3:8
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;
Heb 7:7
And without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better.
All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity.
Mar 4:31
It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when it is sown in the earth, is less than all the seeds that be in the earth:
Ezr 9:13

And after all that is come upon us for our evil deeds, and for our great trespass, seeing that thou our God hast punished us less than our iniquities deserve, and hast given us such deliverance as this; hast
corruption_summary: Less than the least is read as an apostle's false modesty, when it is the true arithmetic of a man who once wasted the church.
corruption_paragraphs: “Less than the least of all saints” is treated as a rhetorical bow, the sort of thing a great man says before accepting the honour. Paul had watched the coats laid down at Stephen's feet. He wrote the phrase as a grammatical impossibility on purpose — a comparative built on a superlative — because his sense of what grace had covered outran the language. The self-esteem gospel calls that unhealthy. Paul called it the reason he could preach the unsearchable riches of Christ without preaching himself, and the chapter shows no sign that the confession slowed him down.

Ezra 9:13 is the confession modern religion cannot make. Punished less than our iniquities deserve: the returned exiles had lost a kingdom, a temple, and two generations, and Ezra says it was less than they had earned. The modern reflex is the reverse — every affliction is an injustice, and God is asked to explain Himself. The man who knows what he deserves finds mercy in what he got; the man who does not finds grievance in everything.
roots_summary: Hebrew me'at (H4592), little, few; ephes (H657), nothing, less than nothing; Greek elachistoteros (G1647), less than the least; elatton (G1640), inferior; mikroteros (G3398), smaller.
roots_lines: Hebrew me'at (H4592) — little, few, less; Exodus 16:17, Exodus 30:15, Numbers 26:54.
Hebrew ephes (H657) — an end, nothing; Isaiah 40:17, “less than nothing.”
Greek elachistoteros (G1647) — less than the least; Ephesians 3:8 only; elatton (G1640), Hebrews 7:7; mikroteros (G3398), Mark 4:31.
usage: “Less than the least of all saints” — a superlative made smaller on purpose.
“The less is blessed of the better” — Melchizedek's rank settled by a blessing.
“Punished us less than our iniquities deserve” — Ezra's arithmetic of mercy.

pos: adj., prep., and n. (gone by; beyond; former time; rendering Hebrew abar, Greek parerchomai, pote, and anexichniastos)
etymology: The old participle of pass. In the Authorized Version the word carries two senses that theology needs: time that has gone, and a thing that lies beyond reach.
biblical_def: God's ways are “past finding out” (Rom 11:33). The Gentiles are “past feeling” and have given themselves over unto lasciviousness (Eph 4:19). The believer's former life is “time past”: “in time past ye walked according to the course of this world” (Eph 2:2); “the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles” (1Pe 4:3). Sarah received strength to conceive “when she was past age” (Heb 11:11). And Jeremiah's saddest sentence: “The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved” (Jer 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines past as gone by; not present; spent; and, as a preposition, beyond in time or degree.
webster_full: PAST, pp. of pass. Gone by; not present; as, past time.
2. Spent; ended; accomplished.
PAST, prep. Beyond in time; beyond in degree; as, past cure; past finding out.
scriptures: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Eph 4:19
Who being past feeling have given themselves over unto lasciviousness, to work all uncleanness with greediness.
Jer 8:20
The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
Eph 2:2
Wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience:
Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age, because she judged him faithful who had promised.
corruption_summary: Past finding out is quoted to stop theology, when Paul wrote it at the end of eleven chapters of it.
corruption_paragraphs: “His ways past finding out” is the verse men reach for to close a discussion of election. Paul wrote it to close Romans 9 to 11 — after three chapters of the most searching argument in the Bible on exactly that subject. The doxology is not a refusal to think; it is what thinking looks like when it reaches the edge. The man who quotes Romans 11:33 before reading Romans 9 has used the exclamation without paying for it.

Ephesians 4:19 names the condition modern culture is most proud of: past feeling. The Greek is a medical word for a limb gone numb. Conscience does not usually die by argument; it dies by use, until the thing that once made a man ashamed makes him nothing at all, and then he is free — free to give himself over. Jeremiah 8:20 is the same numbness seen from the end: a harvest that came and went while the people waited, a summer that ended, and the plain arithmetic, we are not saved. Time past does not return, which is why Peter says the time past may suffice.
roots_summary: Hebrew abar (H5674), to pass over, pass away; Greek parerchomai (G3928), to pass by; pote (G4218), formerly; anexichniastos (G421), untraceable; apalgeo (G524), to cease to feel.
roots_lines: Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over, pass away; Jeremiah 8:20, Genesis 50:4, Song of Solomon 2:11.
Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, go past; 1 Peter 4:3, Matthew 14:15.
Greek anexichniastos (G421) — not to be traced out; Romans 11:33, Ephesians 3:8; apalgeo (G524), past feeling; Ephesians 4:19 only.
usage: “His ways past finding out” — written at the end of the argument, not instead of it.
“Being past feeling” — a conscience gone numb by use.
“The harvest is past, the summer is ended” — and we are not saved.

pos: adv. and adj. (in the same manner; equally; rendering Hebrew yachad and echad; supplied in Romans 14:5)
etymology: Old English gelīc, with the prefix worn down to a-. The Hebrew behind it is usually together: things that come to the same place at once.
biblical_def: To God the darkness and the light “are both alike” (Psa 139:12). “He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works” (Psa 33:15). Under the sun “all things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked” (Ecc 9:2). “Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD” (Pro 20:10). David ruled that the man who tarried by the stuff and the man who went down to the battle “shall part alike” (1Sa 30:24). And Paul: “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines alike as in the same manner, form, or degree; with resemblance; and, as an adjective, having resemblance or similitude.
webster_full: ALIKE, a. Having resemblance or similitude; similar.
ALIKE, adv. In the same manner, form or degree; as, we are all alike concerned in religion.
scriptures: Yea, the darkness hideth not from thee; but the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee.
Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
Ecc 9:2

All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous, and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean, and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth, and to him that sacrificeth not: as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath.
He fashioneth their hearts alike; he considereth all their works.
Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD.
For who will hearken unto you in this matter? but as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike.
corruption_summary: Every day alike is quoted to abolish the Lord's day, and the darkness and the light alike to excuse the deeds of darkness.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 14:5 is the proof-text for a Christianity with no set day, and the word it turns on is not in the Greek. Paul wrote “another esteemeth every day,” and the translators supplied alike in italics to complete the sense. The chapter is about the Jewish calendar of feasts and fasts and the meats attached to them — the things a weak brother's conscience was still bound by — and Paul's rule is forbearance, not abolition. The same apostle kept the first day of the week for the collection and the breaking of bread (1Co 16:2; Act 20:7), and John called it the Lord's day. A verse about not judging your brother over Jewish fast days does not repeal the fourth commandment; it repeals the judging.

Psalm 139:12 is sometimes read as if it meant that God is indifferent to the difference between light and darkness. It means He can see in both. The whole psalm is the impossibility of hiding: the night that a man counts on to cover him shines as the day to the One who fashioned him. Ecclesiastes 9:2 is the other side — under the sun the same event comes to the righteous and the wicked, and the Preacher will not pretend otherwise; the difference is not in the event but in what lies past it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yachad (H3162), together, alike; echad (H259), one, the same; in Romans 14:5 the word is supplied by the translators.
roots_lines: Hebrew yachad (H3162) — together, as one; Psalm 33:15, Deuteronomy 12:22, 1 Samuel 30:24.
Hebrew echad (H259) — one, the same; Ecclesiastes 9:2, “one event.”
Romans 14:5 — krinei pasan hemeran, “esteemeth every day”; alike is the translators' italic supplement.
usage: “The darkness and the light are both alike to thee” — no cover of night before God.
“Esteemeth every day alike” — a supplied word, and a chapter about forbearance.
“They shall part alike” — David's statute for the men who kept the baggage.

pos: n. (privation; that which is lost; damage suffered; rendering Hebrew chata and shekol, Greek zemia and apobole)
etymology: Old English los, destruction. Paul's word, zemia, is the merchant's word for a bad entry in the ledger.
biblical_def: Paul keeps accounts: “what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:7–8). The builder with wood, hay, and stubble “shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire” (1Co 3:15). In the storm Paul promises “there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship” (Act 27:22). Babylon says she shall not know “the loss of children” (Isa 47:8), and it comes in one day. Jacob tells Laban, “That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it” (Gen 31:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loss as privation; the state of being deprived of something; failure; destruction; waste; that which is lost.
webster_full: LOSS, n. Privation; as the loss of property; the loss of health.
2. Destruction; ruin; as the loss of a ship at sea.
3. Defeat; failure; waste; useless application.
4. That which is lost; as, to bear the loss.
scriptures: Php 3:7
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
If any man's work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire.
And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship.
That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it; of my hand didst thou require it, whether stolen by day, or stolen by night.
corruption_summary: All things but loss is admired as Paul's zeal, when it is a ledger entry against the things men still count as gain.
corruption_paragraphs: Philippians 3 is an accountant's page. On one side Paul lists what had been gain — circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless as to the law — and then he moves the whole column to the other side and writes loss against it, and then dung. The modern reading admires the passion and keeps the column where it was. The point is not that Paul felt strongly; it is that everything a religious man counts as credit before God is, for the purpose of being found in Christ, a debit. A righteousness of one's own is not a small asset; it is a loss, because it stands where His righteousness would go.

First Corinthians 3:15 keeps the word from being sentimental in the other direction. A saved man can suffer loss. The foundation is Christ and the builder is saved, but the work is burned and the wages with it — “yet so as by fire,” the way a man escapes a burning house with his life and nothing else. Grace does not make the building material irrelevant; it makes the builder safe while the fire does its audit.
roots_summary: Hebrew chata in the piel (H2398), to bear the loss, make good; shekol (H7908), bereavement; Greek zemia (G2209), loss, damage; zemioo (G2210), to suffer loss; apobole (G580), a casting away.
roots_lines: Hebrew chata, piel (H2398) — to bear the loss of, to make good; Genesis 31:39.
Hebrew shekol (H7908) — bereavement, loss of children; Isaiah 47:8–9.
Greek zemia (G2209) — loss, damage; Philippians 3:7–8, Acts 27:21; zemioo (G2210), 1 Corinthians 3:15; apobole (G580), Acts 27:22.
usage: “I counted loss for Christ” — the whole column moved to the other side.
“He shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved” — a saved builder and a burned building.
“No loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship” — the promise held to the letter.

pos: n. and v. (courage, gladness of heart; to gladden; rendering Greek tharseo and euthumeo, Hebrew samach)
etymology: Old French chiere, the face, from Late Latin cara; good cheer was first a good countenance. The Lord's word behind it, tharseo, is courage.
biblical_def: “Be of good cheer” is the Lord's own formula, said to the palsied man (“Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee,” Mat 9:2), to the disciples on the water (“Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid,” Mat 14:27), to the eleven before the cross (“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world,” John 16:33), and to Paul in the castle at Jerusalem (“Be of good cheer, Paul,” Act 23:11). Paul passes it on in the storm: “be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you” (Act 27:22). The Law gives a newly married man a year at home to “cheer up his wife which he hath taken” (Deu 24:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cheer as a state of gladness or joy; a good state of spirits; and, as a verb, to gladden, to encourage, to inspirit.
webster_full: CHEER, n. A state of gladness or joy; a state of animation, above gloom and depression of spirits, but below mirth.
2. Provisions for a feast; entertainment; as, they made good cheer.
CHEER, v.t. To gladden; to make cheerful; to salute with shouts of joy; to encourage; to inspirit.
scriptures: John 16:33
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
Mat 9:2
And, behold, they brought to him a man sick of the palsy, lying on a bed: and Jesus seeing their faith said unto the sick of the palsy; Son, be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee.
But straightway Jesus spake unto them, saying, Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid.
And the night following the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.
Deu 24:5
When a man hath taken a new wife, he shall not go out to war, neither shall he be charged with any business: but he shall be free at home one year, and shall cheer up his wife which he hath taken.
corruption_summary: Be of good cheer is reduced to cheerfulness, when every time the Lord said it He gave a reason that was not the hearer's feelings.
corruption_paragraphs: In each of the four Gospel sayings the command is followed by a ground, and the ground is never the hearer's circumstances. “Be of good cheer; thy sins be forgiven thee” — to a man who came to be healed and was first pardoned. “Be of good cheer; it is I” — the wind had not dropped. “Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” — said in the sentence that promised tribulation. Positive thinking tells a man to feel better; Christ tells him a fact and lets the courage follow from it. The Greek word is courage, and courage needs a reason.

Acts 23:11 is the night after Paul was nearly torn in pieces by the council, and the Lord's reason is a commission: “as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.” Paul is told he will not die in Jerusalem because there is a work in Rome, and four chapters later, with the ship breaking up under him, he hands the same sentence to two hundred and seventy-six pagans. Good cheer in Scripture is transferable, because it rests on a word given, not on a mood found.
roots_summary: Greek tharseo (G2293), to have courage, be of good cheer; euthumeo (G2114), to be of good spirits; Hebrew samach (H8055), to make glad.
roots_lines: Greek tharseo (G2293) — take courage; Matthew 9:2, 14:27, Mark 6:50, John 16:33, Acts 23:11.
Greek euthumeo (G2114) — to be of good spirit; Acts 27:22, 27:25, James 5:13.
Hebrew samach (H8055) — to rejoice, make glad; Deuteronomy 24:5, “cheer up his wife.”
usage: “Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” — courage with a reason.
“Be of good cheer; it is I” — before the wind dropped.
“Cheer up his wife which he hath taken” — the Law's first year of marriage.

pos: adv. (with great affection; at a high price; in the AV chiefly in the address dearly beloved, rendering Greek agapetos and Hebrew yedidut)
etymology: Old English dēore, precious, costly, and so beloved; the two senses were one word. What is dearly loved is what has cost something.
biblical_def: Dearly stands almost only before beloved, and it is how Paul addresses churches he is about to correct: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves” (Rom 12:19); “Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry” (1Co 10:14); “Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves” (2Co 7:1); “my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved” (Php 4:1). Timothy is “my dearly beloved son” (2Ti 1:2). And God says of Judah, “I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies” (Jer 12:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines dearly as at a high price; with great fondness; with great affection.
webster_full: DEARLY, adv. At a high price; as, he pays dearly for his rashness.
2. With great fondness; as, we love our children dearly.
scriptures: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
Wherefore, my dearly beloved, flee from idolatry.
Having therefore these promises, dearly beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.
Php 4:1
Therefore, my brethren dearly beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, so stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved.
Jer 12:7
I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
corruption_summary: Affection and correction are set against each other, and Paul's dearly beloved is the address on every hard command he wrote.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern pastoral instinct treats warmth and warning as a trade: the more you love a congregation, the less you say. Paul's usage runs the other way. Dearly beloved introduces the command not to avenge, the command to flee idolatry, the command to cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit. The address is not a softener before the blow; it is the reason for the blow. A man does not warn strangers. The church that hears only affection from its pulpit has been told, in the gentlest possible way, that it is not dearly beloved.

Jeremiah 12:7 is the hardest use of the word. “I have forsaken mine house, I have left mine heritage; I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.” God does not stop calling Judah the dearly beloved of His soul in the sentence in which He hands her over. The two things are true at once, and the exile was not the end of the affection but its discipline — the same logic Hebrews 12 applies to every son.
roots_summary: Greek agapetos (G27), beloved, rendered dearly beloved for emphasis; Hebrew yedidut (H3033), the object of love, darling.
roots_lines: Greek agapetos (G27) — beloved; Romans 12:19, 1 Corinthians 10:14, 2 Corinthians 7:1, 12:19, Philippians 4:1, 2 Timothy 1:2, Philemon 1:1.
Hebrew yedidut (H3033) — beloved one, darling; Jeremiah 12:7 only.
usage: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves” — affection as the ground of the command.
“My dearly beloved, flee from idolatry” — a warning to people who were loved.
“The dearly beloved of my soul” — said in the sentence of exile.

pos: pron. (the reflexive and emphatic form of it; in the AV used of the Spirit; rendering Greek autos and heautou)
etymology: It + self. The Authorized Version's neuter for the Holy Spirit in Romans 8 follows the grammar of the Greek noun pneuma, not a judgment about the Spirit's personhood.
biblical_def: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16), and “the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Rom 8:26). “If a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand” (Mar 3:25). “As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (John 15:4). Charity “doth not behave itself unseemly” (1Co 13:5). The body of Christ “maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love” (Eph 4:16). From the first chapter: the earth brought forth the tree “whose seed was in itself” (Gen 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines itself as the neutral reciprocal pronoun, or substitute, applied to things; the thing itself.
webster_full: ITSELF, pron. The neutral reciprocal pronoun, or substitute, applied to things. The thing is good in itself.
scriptures: Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
Rom 8:26
Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
Mar 3:25
And if a house be divided against itself, that house cannot stand.
John 15:4
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
corruption_summary: The Spirit itself is cited to prove the Spirit is a force, when the neuter is the grammar of a noun and the verses give Him the work of a person.
corruption_paragraphs: Anti-trinitarian readers point to “the Spirit itself” as if the translators had ruled the Holy Ghost impersonal. They had done nothing of the kind; they had followed the Greek, where pneuma is neuter and takes a neuter pronoun the way child does. The same chapter gives the Spirit the work only a person can do: He bears witness, He makes intercession, He has a mind (“he that searcheth the hearts knoweth what is the mind of the Spirit,” v. 27), and in John 16 the Lord breaks the grammar on purpose — “when he, the Spirit of truth, is come” — using the masculine of a neuter noun. A pronoun is not a doctrine. The doctrine is in the verbs.

John 15:4 is the sentence self-improvement cannot survive. The branch cannot bear fruit of itself — not will not, cannot — and the Lord applies it without softening: “no more can ye.” Everything the Christian life produces is produced in union, and the moment a man attempts fruit of himself he has answered the question of where the fruit comes from. Mark 3:25 adds the corporate form: a house divided against itself cannot stand, which the Lord said of Satan's kingdom and history has said of every church that forgot it.
roots_summary: Greek autos (G846), self, the same; heautou (G1438), of itself, of himself; Hebrew bo, in it.
roots_lines: Greek autos (G846) — the very one, itself; Romans 8:16, 8:26, auto to pneuma.
Greek heautou (G1438) — of itself; Mark 3:25, John 15:4, Ephesians 4:16, Romans 14:14.
Hebrew bo (H871a) — in it, in itself; Genesis 1:11–12, “whose seed is in itself.”
usage: “The Spirit itself beareth witness” — neuter grammar, personal work.
“The branch cannot bear fruit of itself” — and no more can ye.
“A house divided against itself” — said of Satan's kingdom first.

pos: pron. (the reflexive and emphatic form of she; rendering Greek heautes and Hebrew beqirbah, within her)
etymology: Her + self. The reflexive marks the woman as her own agent: Sarah laughed within herself, the bride made herself ready.
biblical_def: Sarah “laughed within herself” at the promise (Gen 18:12), and Hebrews records the end of the story: “Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed… because she judged him faithful who had promised” (Heb 11:11). The woman with the issue of blood “said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole” (Mat 9:21). The daughter of Abraham bowed together eighteen years “could in no wise lift up herself” (Luk 13:11). Babylon “hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously” (Rev 18:7). And the Lamb's wife “hath made herself ready” (Rev 19:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines herself as the reciprocal form of she, used emphatically or reflexively: she herself; she hurt herself.
webster_full: HERSELF, pron. This denotes a female, the subject of discourse, the same that is the nominative to the verb: she herself.
2. Used reflexively, as the object of the verb: she hurt herself.
scriptures: Through faith also Sara herself received strength to conceive seed, and was delivered of a child when she was past age, because she judged him faithful who had promised.
Rev 19:7
Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.
Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?
Mat 9:21
For she said within herself, If I may but touch his garment, I shall be whole.
And, behold, there was a woman which had a spirit of infirmity eighteen years, and was bowed together, and could in no wise lift up herself.
Rev 18:7
How much she hath glorified herself, and lived deliciously, so much torment and sorrow give her: for she saith in her heart, I sit a queen, and am no widow, and shall see no sorrow.
corruption_summary: The bride making herself ready is read as the church earning its wedding, when the next verse says the garment was granted.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 19:7 says the Lamb's wife hath made herself ready, and verse 8 says how: “to her was granted that she should be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white: for the fine linen is the righteousness of saints.” The readiness is real and the linen is hers, and it was granted. Scripture holds both without strain — the bride does the dressing with a garment she did not weave. The two errors stand on either side: a church that will not make herself ready because everything is grace, and a church that thinks the linen is her own spinning. Babylon in the previous chapter is the second error full grown: she “hath glorified herself.”

Sarah's two verses are the whole doctrine of faith in one woman. She laughed within herself at the promise in Genesis 18; Hebrews 11 says she herself received strength, because she judged Him faithful who had promised. The laugh is not omitted from the record and the faith is not withheld from the credit. Faith in Scripture is not the absence of a laugh; it is the judgment, arrived at after the laugh, that God is faithful.
roots_summary: Greek heautes (G1438), of herself; aute (G846), she herself; Hebrew beqirbah (H7130), in her inward part.
roots_lines: Greek heautes (G1438) — herself; Revelation 19:7, 18:7, Matthew 9:21.
Greek aute (G846) — she herself; Hebrews 11:11, “Sara herself.”
Hebrew qereb (H7130) — the inward part; Genesis 18:12, “laughed within herself.”
usage: “His wife hath made herself ready” — in linen that was granted.
“Sara herself received strength” — the laugh recorded, the faith credited.
“She hath glorified herself” — Babylon's whole biography.

pos: pron. (the possessive of we, standing alone; rendering Greek hemon and hemeteros, Hebrew lanu)
etymology: Our + the possessive s. The word is a claim, and Scripture records it in mouths that had no right to it and in one that did.
biblical_def: The husbandmen say of the heir, “come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours” (Mar 12:7; Luk 20:14). The herdmen of Gerar strive, saying, “The water is ours” (Gen 26:20). Against these Paul writes to the church at Corinth “with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours” (1Co 1:2), tells the Corinthians “we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus” (2Co 1:14), and charges Titus, “let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful” (Tit 3:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives ours as the possessive of we, used when the noun is omitted: this book is ours.
webster_full: OURS, pron. possessive. Of us; belonging to us; used when the noun is omitted; as, this house is ours.
scriptures: Mar 12:7
But those husbandmen said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours.

Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:
Tit 3:14
And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.
As also ye have acknowledged us in part, that we are your rejoicing, even as ye also are ours in the day of the Lord Jesus.
And the herdmen of Gerar did strive with Isaac's herdmen, saying, The water is ours: and he called the name of the well Esek; because they strove with him.
corruption_summary: The inheritance shall be ours is the sentence under every theft of what is Christ's, and Paul's ours is the church He owns.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the husbandmen is the history of religion run by men for themselves. The vineyard was let out; the fruit was due; the servants were beaten; and when the son came the tenants reasoned, “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours.” Every attempt to hold the church, the ministry, or the Scriptures as a possession rather than a trust says the same sentence more politely. The Lord's application in Mark 12:9 is the answer to all of them: “he will come and destroy the husbandmen, and will give the vineyard unto others.”

Paul's ours is the opposite kind of claim. “Both theirs and ours” in 1 Corinthians 1:2 is the Lord Jesus, confessed by the church in every place — the one possession that cannot be seized because it is held by being had by Him. And Titus 3:14, “let ours also learn to maintain good works,” is the apostle's shorthand for the people of God: ours, not as property, but as family for whom one is answerable.
roots_summary: Greek hemon (G2257), of us; hemeteros (G2251), our own; Hebrew lanu, to us, ours.
roots_lines: Greek hemon (G2257) — of us, ours; Mark 12:7, Luke 20:14, 1 Corinthians 1:2, 2 Corinthians 1:14.
Greek hemeteros (G2251) — our own; Titus 3:14, Acts 2:11.
Hebrew lanu (H3807a with suffix) — to us; Genesis 26:20, “The water is ours.”
usage: “The inheritance shall be ours” — the husbandmen's plan, and every theft after it.
“Both theirs and ours” — one Lord held in every place.
“Let ours also learn to maintain good works” — the apostle's family word for the church.

pos: pron. (the possessive of you, standing alone; rendering Greek humon and humeteros, Hebrew lakem)
etymology: Your + the possessive s. In the mouth of God the word is a deed of gift; in the mouth of Jahaziel it is a transfer of the battle.
biblical_def: “Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; and ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's” (1Co 3:21–23). To Jehoshaphat's army: “Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15). To the poor disciples: “Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God” (Luk 6:20). To the eleven: “if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also” (John 15:20). To Israel: “Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours” (Deu 11:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives yours as the possessive of you, used when the noun is omitted: this book is yours.
webster_full: YOURS, pron. possessive. Belonging to you; used when the noun is omitted; as, this book is yours.
scriptures: Therefore let no man glory in men. For all things are yours;
Whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours;

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
Luk 6:20
And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said, Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God.
John 15:20
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea shall your coast be.
corruption_summary: All things are yours is preached as a promise of possessions, when Paul wrote it to end the Corinthians' party spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: “All things are yours” is the prosperity preacher's favourite half-sentence, and it sits in an argument against boasting in men. The Corinthians were saying I am of Paul, I of Apollos, each party claiming a teacher; Paul turns the claim inside out. You do not belong to Paul; Paul belongs to you — and Apollos, and Cephas, and the world, and life, and death. The list is not a catalogue of things to be acquired but a proof that the man in Christ already owns more than any faction could offer him. And the chain ends where every Christian claim must: “ye are Christ's; and Christ is God's.” Everything is yours because you are not your own.

Second Chronicles 20:15 moves the battle out of the hearer's hands. Jehoshaphat had fasted and prayed and confessed, “neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee,” and the answer through Jahaziel was a change of ownership: the battle is not yours, but God's. Judah still marched, still stood, still sang; what they did not do was fight. The modern reading turns the verse into passivity; the chapter shows obedience with the outcome removed from the obeyer's account.
roots_summary: Greek humon (G5216), of you; humeteros (G5212), your own; Hebrew lakem, to you, yours.
roots_lines: Greek humon (G5216) — of you, yours; 1 Corinthians 3:21–22.
Greek humeteros (G5212) — your own; Luke 6:20, John 15:20.
Hebrew lakem (H3807a with suffix) — to you; Deuteronomy 11:24, 2 Chronicles 20:15, “the battle is not yours, but God's.”
usage: “All things are yours; and ye are Christ's” — the chain that ends every party.
“The battle is not yours, but God's” — obedience with the outcome removed from your account.
“Yours is the kingdom of God” — said to the poor.

pos: pron. (the possessive of they, standing alone; rendering Greek auton, Hebrew lahem)
etymology: Their + the possessive s. Twice in the Beatitudes the word carries the kingdom.
biblical_def: The first and last Beatitudes end in it: “Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:3), and “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Mat 5:10). Abram is told that his seed “shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs” (Gen 15:13). Aaron and his sons are girded, “and the priest's office shall be theirs for a perpetual statute” (Exo 29:9). Ezekiel's priests eat the meat offering and the sin offering, “and every dedicated thing in Israel shall be theirs” (Eze 44:29). Paul's Lord is confessed by all that call upon His name, “both theirs and ours” (1Co 1:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives theirs as the possessive of they, used when the noun is omitted: the house is theirs.
webster_full: THEIRS, pron. possessive. Of them; belonging to them; used when the noun is omitted; as, the land is theirs.
scriptures: Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
And he said unto Abram, Know of a surety that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs, and shall serve them; and they shall afflict them four hundred years;
Exo 29:9
And thou shalt gird them with girdles, Aaron and his sons, and put the bonnets on them: and the priest's office shall be theirs for a perpetual statute: and thou shalt consecrate Aaron and his sons.

Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:
corruption_summary: The kingdom is promised to the poor in spirit in the present tense, and the modern reading makes poverty of spirit a mood rather than a verdict on oneself.
corruption_paragraphs: The seven Beatitudes between the first and the last are future — shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be filled — and the two that bracket them are present: theirs is the kingdom. The poor in spirit and the persecuted have it now. Poverty of spirit is not low self-esteem, which is a feeling about oneself; it is bankruptcy before God, which is a judgment about oneself, and the man who has reached that judgment is the man to whom the kingdom is already given. The gospel of self-worth cannot preach the first Beatitude, because the first Beatitude is the end of self-worth and the beginning of Christ's.

Genesis 15:13 pairs the word with a promise that hurt. Abram's seed would be strangers in a land that is not theirs, four hundred years, and afflicted — and the sentence is part of the covenant, not an interruption of it. Scripture never pretends that the people of God own the ground they stand on in this age. What is theirs is the office (Exo 29:9), the dedicated things (Eze 44:29), and the kingdom (Mat 5:3); what is not theirs, for now, is the land they are passing through.
roots_summary: Greek auton (G846), of them; Hebrew lahem, to them, theirs.
roots_lines: Greek auton (G846) — of them, theirs; Matthew 5:3, 5:10, 1 Corinthians 1:2.
Hebrew lahem (H3807a with suffix) — to them; Genesis 15:13, Exodus 29:9, Ezekiel 44:29.
usage: “Theirs is the kingdom of heaven” — present tense, said twice.
“A land that is not theirs” — the covenant's honest clause.
“The priest's office shall be theirs” — a possession that was a charge.
